text: Pterosaurs were flying [[reptile|reptiles]] that lived alongside the dinosaurs. They were close cousins of dinosaurs, but they were not dinosaurs. They were the first animals with backbones to fly by flapping, in the Late Triassic, more than 215 million years ago.

Their wing was skin and muscle held out by one enormously long fourth finger, stretching back to the leg. Birds use feathers; bats use several fingers. The biggest, [[@flying-reptiles-quetzal|Quetzalcoatlus]], had wings about 10 metres across, close to the wingspan of a small plane.

sec.t:
Scientists sort animals by their family tree, not just by looks. Dinosaurs share certain features of the hip and legs, which hold their legs straight under the body. Pterosaurs don't have them.

The two groups split from a shared ancestor before either appeared, more than 240 million years ago. Think of them as cousins who grew up in the same neighbourhood. The flying animals that really are dinosaurs are [[@birds-dinosaurs|birds]], which [[evolve|evolved]] feathered wings separately, much later.

A pterosaur's arm ended in three small clawed fingers and one huge fourth finger. In big [[species|species]], that single finger could be longer than the rest of the animal's body. A flap of skin, strengthened with thin fibres, ran from it to the hind leg.

The skin could tighten and loosen, a bit like a sail. Unlike a bird's feathers, it was alive, with muscles and blood vessels. Their bones were hollow and thin-walled, so even giants were light for their size. That is the same trick that keeps [[@airplanes-fly|aeroplanes]] light: strong tubes rather than solid bars.

On the ground, pterosaurs walked on four limbs. [[fossil|Fossil]] footprints from France, the western USA and elsewhere show small hand prints beside longer foot prints. The long wing finger folded back out of the way, and the animal walked on its knuckles and feet.

Those tracks settled an old argument. Some scientists had once pictured pterosaurs crawling clumsily, or hanging from cliffs like bats.

Many pterosaurs lived by the sea and caught fish, perhaps skimming the surface. Pterodaustro, from Argentina, had hundreds of thin, bristle-like teeth, probably used to strain tiny food from water, much like flamingos do today.

Many pterosaurs had a fuzzy coat of fine fibres called pycnofibres. Some had bony head crests, which may have helped them show off.

The first pterosaur fossil was described in 1784 from limestone in Germany. At first nobody knew what it was: some thought it was a swimming animal. In 1828, [[@mary-anning|Mary Anning]] found the first pterosaur skeleton in Britain, on the cliffs at Lyme Regis.

Pterosaurs survived for about 150 million years. They vanished 66 million years ago with the non-bird dinosaurs, when [[@extinction|the asteroid]] hit. Today the skies belong to birds and bats, two very different answers to the same problem.

sec.t:
ज़्यादातर पौधे अपने तने की नोक से बढ़ते हैं। घास अलग है। उसका बढ़ने वाला हिस्सा नीचे, मिट्टी के पास होता है, और हर पत्ती नीचे से ऊपर धकेली जाती है। हिरन ऊपर का हिस्सा काट ले, तो पौधा बस बढ़ता रहता है।

बहुत-सी घासें ज़मीन के नीचे के तनों से भी फैलती हैं, जिन्हें [[rhizome|प्रकंद]] कहते हैं, और उनकी जड़ें मिट्टी में गहरे तक जा सकती हैं। जब घास के मैदान में आग फैलती है, तो ऊपर का हिस्सा जल जाता है, पर जड़ें और बढ़ने वाले हिस्से ज़मीन के नीचे बचे रहते हैं। बारिश के कुछ ही हफ़्तों में ताज़ी हरी कोंपलें निकल आती हैं।

इसी मज़बूती की वजह से घास के मैदान विशाल झुंडों का पेट भर सकते हैं। अफ़्रीका के [[@serengeti|सेरेंगेटी]] में दस लाख से ज़्यादा वाइल्डबीस्ट हर साल बारिश के पीछे-पीछे घास के मैदानों में घूमते हैं।

{{story:cheetah-return}}

घास सिर्फ़ गायों और वाइल्डबीस्ट का पेट नहीं भरती। [[@rice|चावल]], गेहूँ, मक्का, जौ, जई और रागी-बाजरा जैसे [[@millets|मोटे अनाज]], सब घास हैं। इनके दाने उगाना और काटना इंसानों ने हज़ारों साल पहले सीखा। गन्ना एक विशाल घास है, और बाँस तो सबसे बड़ी घास है।

दुनिया की कुछ सबसे [[fertile|उपजाऊ]] खेती की ज़मीन कभी घास का मैदान थी। अमेरिकी प्रेयरी और यूक्रेन के स्टेपी की गहरी, काली मिट्टी हज़ारों सालों में घास की जड़ों के उगने और सड़ने से बनी।

sec.h: भारत के भूले हुए घास के मैदान
sec.t:
भारत के घास के मैदानों पर अक्सर ध्यान ही नहीं दिया गया। बरसों तक कुछ सरकारी नक्शों में खुले घास के मैदानों को "बंजर ज़मीन" लिखा गया, और कुछ पर पेड़ लगा दिए गए या खेत बना दिए गए। जबकि यहाँ ऐसे जानवर रहते हैं जो और कहीं नहीं मिलते।

गोडावण, यानी ग्रेट इंडियन बस्टर्ड, उड़ने वाले सबसे भारी पक्षियों में से एक है। यह राजस्थान और गुजरात के सूखे घास के मैदानों में रहता है। हाल के अनुमानों के मुताबिक जंगल में सिर्फ़ लगभग 150 बचे हैं। काले हिरन, [[@wolves-india|भारतीय भेड़िये]], लोमड़ियाँ, खरमोर जैसे फ़्लोरिकन पक्षी और बहुत-से कीड़ों को भी खुली घास चाहिए। 2022 में भारत अफ़्रीका से [[@cheetah-return|चीते]] लाकर मध्य प्रदेश के कूनो नेशनल पार्क में लाया, जहाँ खुले घास के मैदान भी हैं और जंगल भी।

उत्तरी अमेरिका की प्रेयरी में कभी करोड़ों बाइसन थे, शायद 3 से 6 करोड़। 1800 के दशक में शिकारियों ने उन्हें भारी तादाद में मारा। कभी खाल के लिए, कभी शौक के लिए, और कभी उन मूल अमेरिकी कबीलों को भूखा मारने के लिए जो उन पर निर्भर थे। 1880 के दशक के आखिर तक एक हज़ार से भी कम बचे थे।

संरक्षण के काम ने धीरे-धीरे [[@bison-return|बाइसन]] को वापस लौटाया। आज उत्तरी अमेरिका में लाखों बाइसन हैं, ज़्यादातर फ़ार्मों पर, और येलोस्टोन जैसे पार्कों में छोटे जंगली झुंड भी। चरते हुए बाइसन घास को छाँटकर और मिट्टी को उलट-पलटकर प्रेयरी की मदद करते हैं, जैसे दूसरी जगहों पर जंगली झुंड करते हैं।

sec.h: घास के मैदान ज़रूरी क्यों हैं
sec.t:
घास के मैदान धरती की ज़मीन का बड़ा हिस्सा घेरते हैं। सवाना और झाड़ीदार इलाकों को जोड़ लें तो कुछ गिनतियों के हिसाब से लगभग दो-पाँचवाँ हिस्सा। ये अपनी जड़ों और मिट्टी में भारी मात्रा में कार्बन जमा रखते हैं, कभी-कभी जंगलों से भी ज़्यादा सुरक्षित ढंग से, क्योंकि आग घास को जलाती है, ज़मीन के नीचे के भंडार को नहीं।

ये तेज़ी से ग़ायब भी हो रहे हैं। कहीं इन्हें फ़सलों के लिए जोता जा रहा है, कहीं इमारतें बन रही हैं, कहीं ज़रूरत से ज़्यादा चराई हो रही है। वैज्ञानिक कहते हैं कि इन्हें बचाने के लिए इन्हें अपने आप में कीमती जगह मानना होगा, न कि ख़ाली ज़मीन जो कुछ और बनने का इंतज़ार कर रही है।

text: It depends on how you measure. [[@mountaineering|Mount Everest]], on the border of Nepal and China, has the highest summit above sea level: 8,848.86 m. That makes it the highest mountain on Earth.

But Mauna Kea in Hawaii is taller from bottom to top. It rises about 10,200 m from its base on the floor of the Pacific Ocean, though most of it is underwater. And if you measure from the centre of the Earth, the summit of Chimborazo in Ecuador reaches farthest out into space.

sec.t:
Everest sits in the Himalaya, which formed when India crashed slowly into Asia. In Nepal the mountain is called Sagarmatha, and in Tibet, Chomolungma.

In 2020, survey teams from Nepal and China announced a new joint measurement: 8,848.86 m. A Chinese team had carried instruments to the top that year, while Nepali surveyors had climbed it in 2019. Both used satellites and ground measurements. [[@earthquakes|Earthquakes]] and the slow push of India northward can change the height very slightly.

Mauna Kea is a [[@volcano|volcano]] on the Big Island of [[@hawaii-islands|Hawaii]]. It began on the dark floor of the Pacific Ocean, around 6,000 m down, and slowly built itself up from layer after layer of [[lava|lava]]. Its summit is about 4,200 m above sea level, so from a beach it doesn't look nearly as big as Everest.

Measured from base to peak, though, it is about 10,200 m tall, more than 1,300 m taller than Everest. Its summit has some of the world's most important [[@telescopes-how|telescopes]], because the air there is thin, dry and clear. The mountain is also sacred to many Native Hawaiians, and building more telescopes there has caused long disagreements.

Earth isn't a perfect ball. Its spin makes it bulge at the [[equator|equator]], so the ground there is farther from the centre than at the poles. Chimborazo, a volcano in Ecuador, sits almost on the equator.

Its summit is only about 6,260 m above sea level, but it is about 2 km farther from Earth's centre than Everest's peak. If you want to be as close to the stars as possible while standing on Earth, Chimborazo is the place.

[[@sikkim|Kangchenjunga]], on the border of India and Nepal, is India's highest mountain at 8,586 m, and the third highest on Earth. India's official maps also claim K2, the second highest, but it lies in the part of Kashmir run by Pakistan. The people of Sikkim consider it sacred, and many climbers stop just short of the very top out of respect.

In North America, the highest mountain is Denali in [[@alaska|Alaska]], about 6,190 m high. In 2015, the US Geological Survey measured it again with modern equipment and found it was about 3 m shorter than people had thought.

The tallest known mountain in the [[solar-system|solar system]] is [[@space-weird-tallest-mountain|Olympus Mons]] on Mars, a giant volcano about 22 km high, more than twice the height of Mauna Kea from base to peak. It is so wide that if you stood on its slopes, the peak would be hidden beyond the horizon. [[@mars-rovers|Mars rovers]] haven't visited it yet, but spacecraft have photographed it from above.

text: The tallest mountain we know of is Olympus Mons, a giant volcano on Mars. It rises about 22 km above the planet's average surface level. That is two and a half Everests stacked on top of each other, and about twice as high as passenger jets fly.

It is also enormous across. Its base is about 600 km wide, covering an area nearly as big as Maharashtra, or the US state of Arizona. At the top sits a [[crater|crater]] about 80 km long, big enough to swallow the whole of Mumbai with room to spare.

There is one rival. On the [[asteroid|asteroid]] Vesta, a peak in the middle of a giant crater called Rheasilvia stands roughly as tall. Which is higher depends on where you decide each mountain starts.

st.prompt: Why could a volcano on Mars grow so much taller than any on Earth?

options.t: Mars has weaker gravity and its crust does not drift over hot spots
Mars has more volcanoes than Earth
Martian lava is thicker and colder

st.reveal: On Earth, moving plates carry the crust away from a hot spot, so new volcanoes form in a line. On Mars the crust stayed put, and lava kept piling up in one place. Weaker gravity helped the mountain hold up its own weight.

d.try: Pour a spoonful of honey slowly onto a plate in one spot and watch it spread into a wide, low dome. Then slide the plate a little while pouring and see how you get a row of small mounds instead. That is the difference between Mars and Hawaii.
myth: Mount Everest is the tallest mountain anywhere.
Everest has the highest summit above sea level on Earth, at 8,849 m. Mauna Kea in Hawaii is taller from its base on the sea floor, and Olympus Mons on Mars is more than twice Everest's height.
facts: about 22 km above Mars's average surface level
about 80 km by 60 km, up to 3 km deep

sec.t:
Olympus Mons is a shield volcano. Runny [[lava|lava]] flowed out over millions of years and spread into a broad, gentle dome. Most of its slope is only a few degrees steep, gentler than many wheelchair ramps.

That makes for a strange view. If you stood near the base, you could not see the summit at all. The mountain is so wide that the curve of Mars bends it out of sight. Climbing it would feel less like scaling a peak and more like a very long uphill walk lasting weeks.

The edges are a different story. Around much of the base runs a cliff up to 8 km high, almost as tall as Everest by itself. Giant landslides once tumbled off these cliffs, spreading rubble hundreds of kilometres across the plains.

{{story:volcano}}

Earth has shield volcanoes too. The [[@hawaii-islands|islands of Hawaii]] were built by them. But Earth's crust is broken into plates that slowly drift. As a plate slides over a hot spot deep below, old volcanoes get carried away and new ones pop up. That is why Hawaii is a chain of islands rather than one giant mountain.

Mars has no moving plates like ours. Its crust sat still over the hot spot, and lava kept pouring out in the same place for a very long time. The pile just grew and grew.

[[@gravity-planets|Gravity]] helps as well. Mars pulls with only about 38% of Earth's [[gravity|gravity]]. A huge mountain weighs less there, so the rock beneath it can hold up a much taller pile before it sags.

Olympus Mons is quiet now. Some of its lava flows look young for a planet, perhaps a few million years old, though scientists are still working out exact ages. Mars has cooled a great deal inside, so a big eruption today seems unlikely. Mars still shakes now and then, though. NASA's InSight lander recorded more than 1,300 marsquakes between 2018 and 2022.

Spacecraft circling Mars have mapped it in fine detail. The European Space Agency's Mars Express and NASA orbiters have photographed its cliffs and landslides. Some of its slopes show ancient lava channels and signs that [[glacier|glaciers]] may once have crept down its sides.

On Earth, the answer to "tallest mountain" depends on the question. Everest has the highest summit above sea level. But Mauna Kea in Hawaii starts deep on the ocean floor and rises about 10 km in total, so it is taller from base to top. You can compare the contenders in [[@mountains-tallest|the world's tallest mountains]].

And the strangest rival of all? Vesta's peak sits on a lumpy space rock only about 525 km wide, one of the biggest objects in the [[asteroidbelt|asteroid belt]]. Find out just how big they get in [[@asteroid-size|how big asteroids can be]].

text: Sound moves through air as waves of squeezed and stretched air, spreading out like ripples on a pond. At sea level, sound travels at about 343 metres a second, around 1,235 km/h. That's fast, but jets can go faster.

When a plane flies slower than sound, its pressure waves race ahead of it. When it flies faster than sound, the waves can't get out of the way. They pile up into a cone-shaped shock wave trailing behind the plane. When that cone sweeps over you, the air pressure jumps suddenly and then drops. Your ears hear a loud double bang: a sonic boom.

st.prompt: A supersonic jet flies across the whole of India. Who hears its sonic boom?

options.t: People all along its path, as the boom sweeps over them
Only people near where it first went faster than sound
Nobody, because the boom stays behind the plane forever

st.reveal: As long as the plane flies faster than sound, it drags a cone of squeezed air behind it. Wherever that cone touches the ground, people hear a boom, so a long flight leaves a "boom carpet" many kilometres wide.

d.try: Drag your finger slowly through still water in a basin, then quickly. At high speed, the ripples pile up into a V-shaped wake behind your finger. A sonic boom is a 3D version of that V, made of squashed air instead of water.
myth: A sonic boom happens only once, at the moment a plane breaks the sound barrier.

sec.t:
In the 1940s, many pilots feared that planes would shake apart near the speed of sound. Some test planes had wobbled badly as they got close.

On 14 October 1947, the American pilot Chuck Yeager flew a rocket plane called the Bell X-1 over the Mojave Desert in California. It was dropped from under a big bomber and lit its rocket engines. Yeager reached about 1.06 times the speed of sound, now called Mach 1.06. The plane didn't shake apart. People on the ground heard a boom, the first from a plane flying level faster than sound. The orange X-1 now hangs in the Smithsonian in Washington, DC.

sec.h: A crack you can make yourself

sec.t:
From 1976 to 2003, the British-French Concorde carried passengers at about twice the speed of sound. It could fly from London to New York in about three and a half hours, roughly half the usual time.

But it was loud. In 1973, the USA banned civil planes from flying faster than sound over land, because booms rattled windows and startled people and animals. Many other countries made similar rules. So Concorde could only go supersonic over the ocean. It was costly to run, and after a crash in 2000 and a slump in air travel, it was retired in 2003.

sec.h: The cloud that isn't a boom
sec.t:
You may have seen photos of a jet wrapped in a white cone of cloud. It looks like the moment of breaking the sound barrier, but it isn't quite. The cloud is water vapour condensing as air pressure drops around the plane. It can happen just below the speed of sound, in damp air.

Fighter jets of the [[@indian-air-force|Indian Air Force]], such as the Rafale and Sukhoi Su-30MKI, can fly at close to twice the speed of sound. Pilots usually do this high up or over the sea, so booms don't disturb towns.

NASA has built a strange-looking jet called the X-59, with a nose about a third of its length. Its shape is designed to spread out the shock waves so that people on the ground hear a soft "thump" rather than a boom. It made its first flight on 28 October 2025.

If tests go well, rules might change and supersonic travel over land could return. Meanwhile, look up after a jet passes and you might see long white lines across the sky. They have nothing to do with booms at all. They're [[@sky-contrails|contrails]], made of ice crystals.

text: Nature's record-breakers come in every size. The blue whale is the largest animal known, up to about 30 m long, as long as three city buses. [[@sky-peregrine|The peregrine falcon]] is the fastest, diving at more than 300 km/h. A tiny dung beetle can pull over a thousand times its own weight, and the [[@extreme-longest-living|Greenland shark]] may live for hundreds of years.

Each record is a clue about how animals have adapted to survive. But records are hard to measure in the wild. Scientists can't easily clock a wild cheetah or weigh a whale, so many numbers are estimates, and some get revised as better tools come along.

st.prompt: Which of these is the fastest animal on Earth?

options.t: The peregrine falcon, diving

st.reveal: A peregrine falcon folds its wings and dives on prey at more than 300 km/h. A cheetah tops out at around 100 km/h. Claims of sailfish reaching over 100 km/h come from old, doubtful measurements.

myth: A cheetah can keep running at top speed for a long way.

sec.t:
The [[@blue-whale|blue whale]] is probably the heaviest animal that has ever lived, heavier than even the largest dinosaurs as far as we can tell. A big one can weigh well over 100 tonnes. Its heart alone can weigh about 180 kg, as much as two grown men, and its main food is krill, shrimp-like animals only a few centimetres long.

On land, the African elephant is the heaviest animal, and [[@power-giraffe-neck|the giraffe]] is the tallest, reaching more than 5 m. In India, the Asian elephant is the biggest land animal, and [[@wild-indian-gaur|the gaur]], or Indian bison, is the largest wild cattle in the world. The king cobra, found in India's forests, is the longest venomous snake, sometimes over 5 m long.

At the other end of the scale, some frogs from Papua New Guinea are smaller than 1 cm when fully grown, short enough to sit on your fingernail with room to spare. The bee hummingbird of Cuba, [[@extreme-smallest-animals|the smallest bird]], is about 5–6 cm long, beak and all.

[[@sky-arctic-tern|The Arctic tern]] makes the longest known migration. It flies from the Arctic to the Antarctic and back every year, and tracking tags show some birds cover more than 70,000 km in a single round trip.

For its size, one of the strongest animals ever measured is a horned dung beetle. In one study, a male pulled a weight more than 1,000 times its own body weight. That is like a person pulling six double-decker buses.

Other animals are record-breaking survivors. [[@extreme-toughest-animal|Tardigrades]], tiny animals less than 1 mm long, can survive being dried out for years and have even survived being exposed to space. Bar-headed geese fly over the Himalaya, where the air has less than half the oxygen found at sea level.

In 2016, scientists in Denmark worked out the ages of Greenland sharks by studying the lenses of their eyes. The lens contains [[protein|proteins]] that form before birth and never change. The biggest shark they studied was estimated to be at least 272 years old, and possibly closer to 400.

Some other animals live astonishingly long too. [[@turtles-tortoises|Giant tortoises]] can pass 150 years, and some bowhead whales seem to have lived more than 200 years. People also love keeping [[@world-records|world records]], but in the animal kingdom, the record books keep changing as scientists measure more.

text: A fridge works by moving heat, not by making cold. Inside its pipes is a special liquid called a [[refrigerant|refrigerant]], which boils at very low temperatures. As it boils inside the fridge, it soaks up heat from your food and the air around it.

A pump called a compressor then squeezes the refrigerant gas, making it hot. The hot gas flows through coils on the back or bottom of the fridge, where it gives its heat to the kitchen and turns back into a liquid. Then it flows back inside to boil again.
Round and round it goes, carrying heat out of the box all day and night. That is why the back of a fridge feels warm.

st.prompt: If you leave the fridge door open on a hot day, what happens to the kitchen?

options.t: It gets slightly warmer
It cools down like an air conditioner
Nothing changes

st.reveal: The fridge pulls heat from the air at the front but dumps even more heat out of the back, because the motor adds heat of its own. With the door open, the kitchen ends up a little warmer.

d.try: Wet one wrist and leave the other dry, then gently blow on both. The wet one feels colder because evaporating water carries heat away. A fridge uses the same trick with a special liquid, over and over again in a loop.
myth: An open fridge can cool down a hot room.
A fridge only moves heat from inside to the coils outside. With the door open, it moves heat around the same room while its motor adds extra heat. The room gets warmer, not cooler.

sec.h: The cooling trick you already know
sec.t:
When you climb out of a swimming pool on a windy day, you shiver. As water on your skin evaporates, it carries heat away with it. [[@sweat|Sweat]] cools you the same way. Turning a liquid into a gas always needs heat, and it takes that heat from whatever is nearby.

A clay matka uses this idea to keep drinking water cool. Water seeps through tiny pores and evaporates from the outside, chilling the rest, as explained in [[@evaporation-cooling|how a clay pot cools water]].

A fridge does this in a closed loop. Its refrigerant evaporates in pipes inside the fridge, pulling heat from the food. Then the compressor squashes it back into a liquid outside, where the heat escapes. No liquid is lost, so it can keep going for years.

Follow the refrigerant on one trip around:

1. The **evaporator** is a set of cold pipes inside the fridge. Here the refrigerant boils and soaks up heat.
2. The **compressor**, the humming motor near the bottom, squeezes the warm gas so it gets hotter still.
3. The **condenser coils** on the back release that heat into the kitchen. The gas cools and becomes a liquid again.
4. The **expansion valve** is a narrow gap. The liquid sprays through, its pressure drops suddenly, and it becomes very cold, ready to start again.

A thermostat switches the compressor on and off to keep the inside at about 4°C. The freezer is kept near –18°C.

For thousands of years, people kept food cool with cellars, clay pots, snow and salt. In ancient Persia, people built tall domed ice houses called yakhchals, which kept ice into the hot summer.

In the 1800s, ice became a business. In 1833, a ship from Boston carrying ice cut from frozen New England lakes reached Calcutta, now [[@kolkata|Kolkata]], after a voyage of about four months. Much of it melted on the way, but enough survived to sell. Ice houses were soon built in Indian port cities.

Jacob Perkins, an American living in Britain, patented a machine in 1834 that used the compression idea fridges still use. Home fridges spread across the US in the 1920s and 1930s, and across India much later.

{{story:frozen-food}}

sec.h: Einstein's fridge and the ozone hole
sec.t:
In 1930, Albert [[@einstein|Einstein]] and the physicist Leo Szilard patented a fridge with no moving parts. They had read about a family harmed by gas leaking from a faulty fridge seal. Their design was never widely used, but it shows how many clever minds have worked on cooling.

Many early fridges used dangerous gases. In the 1930s, chemicals called CFCs replaced them because they were safe to breathe. Decades later, scientists found that CFCs drifting into the sky were destroying the [[@ozone-layer|ozone layer]], which shields us from harmful sunlight.

In 1987, countries agreed to the Montreal Protocol, phasing out CFCs. Every member of the United Nations has since joined it. Today many fridges use other refrigerants, including isobutane.

India has fridges that need no electricity at all. In Gujarat, a potter named Mansukhbhai Prajapati designed the Mitticool, a clay fridge cooled by evaporating water. And the strangest part? An air conditioner is basically a fridge turned inside out, cooling your room instead of a box, as you can find in [[@air-conditioning|how air conditioning works]].

text: Seeing feels effortless, but it isn't simple. Your eyes catch patterns of light, and your brain has to turn them into a world of objects, distances and colours. It does this very fast by using shortcuts, rules of thumb learned over millions of years and over your own lifetime.

Most of the time, those shortcuts work beautifully. An optical illusion is a picture designed so that the shortcuts give the wrong answer. Two lines look different lengths when they're the same. A still drawing seems to move. Two squares look different colours when they're printed with exactly the same ink.
Illusions aren't signs that your eyes are broken. They show how hard your brain is working behind the scenes.

st.prompt: The full Moon is rising and looks enormous over the rooftops. You take a photo, then another when it is high in the sky. How do they compare?

Both Moons are the same size in the photos

st.reveal: The Moon is the same size in both photos. In fact it is very slightly further from you when it's on the horizon. The giant Moon is made by your brain, though scientists still argue about exactly why.

sec.h: The brain fills in the gaps
sec.t:
Your [[@eyes-see|eyes]] send your brain a lot of information, but not everything. Each eye even has a blind spot where the nerve leaves the back of the eye, and there are no light-sensing cells. You never notice it because your [[@brain-works|brain]] fills in the gap with whatever seems likely.

The brain also uses past experience. It knows that things further away look smaller, that light usually comes from above, and that shadows make things darker. It applies these rules automatically, even when you know a picture is a trick. That's why an illusion keeps working after someone explains it to you.

In 1995, Edward Adelson, a scientist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, made a picture of a chessboard with a green cylinder casting a shadow on it. One square in the light looks dark grey. Another square in the shadow looks light grey. They are exactly the same shade. Your brain "corrects" for the shadow, the way it does in real life.

In February 2015, a photo of a striped dress spread across the internet. Some people saw it as blue and black. Others were sure it was white and gold. The real dress was blue and black. Scientists think people's brains made different guesses about whether the dress was in bluish shade or yellowish light, and corrected the colours differently.

For thousands of years, people have noticed that the rising full Moon looks huge over the horizon and smaller when high in the sky. Photos show it's the same size. It is even a tiny bit further away when it's rising.

Nobody is completely sure why the illusion happens. One idea is that the brain sees the sky as a flattened dome and thinks the horizon is further away, so it enlarges the Moon there. Another is that trees and buildings next to the Moon make it seem big by comparison. Artists use similar tricks of size and distance in [[@perspective|perspective]] drawing, and [[@pop-magic-shows|magicians]] use the brain's guesses in their [[@magic-tricks|tricks]].

text: At the front of most TV remotes is a small bulb called an LED. When you press a button, a chip inside the remote makes the LED flash in a very fast pattern of pulses. The light is [[infrared|infrared]], just beyond the red end of the colours we can see, so to your eyes nothing seems to happen.

The [[@television-invented|television]] has a [[sensor|sensor]] that watches for these flashes. Each button has its own pattern, a bit like Morse code, so the TV can tell "volume up" from "channel 7". The whole message takes a fraction of a second.

st.prompt: An early remote from 1955 used a beam of ordinary visible light. What went wrong?

options.t: Sunshine falling on the TV could change the channel
The light made people's eyes water
It only worked at night

st.reveal: The TV had light sensors in its corners and couldn't tell a remote's beam from sunlight. A bright afternoon could switch channels by itself. Modern remotes avoid this by using infrared light that flickers at a set speed, which sunlight doesn't do.

d.try: Point a TV remote at a phone camera and look at the screen while you press a button. You should see a little light blinking at the front of the remote. If you see nothing, try the phone's other camera, because some have filters that block infrared.
myth: You have to point the remote straight at the TV, or it won't work.
Infrared light bounces off walls, ceilings and even windows. You can often aim at the wall behind you and the TV still changes channel.
facts: its own pattern of on and off pulses

sec.t:
Inside the remote is a grid of rubber buttons sitting over a [[circuit|circuit]] board. Pressing one squeezes a dot of carbon onto two metal tracks and completes a circuit. The chip notices which button closed, looks up its code and starts flashing.

That code is a string of on and off pulses, which engineers treat as [[@binary-code|binary code]]: ones and zeros. A typical message first says "this is for a TV made by this company" and then "this is the button". That is why a remote for one brand usually does nothing to another brand's TV, and why "universal" remotes store hundreds of codes.

If you hold a button down, the remote keeps sending a short "still pressed" signal, which is how the volume keeps climbing. Air conditioners work the same way, but their remotes send the whole setting each time: temperature, fan speed and mode together. That way, if one message is missed, the next press puts everything right.

{{story:binary-code}}

Sunlight, lamps and fires all give off infrared light too. If the TV just looked for "some infrared", it would get confused all day. So the remote's light flickers on and off thousands of times a second, often about 38,000 times, even within a single pulse.

The sensor in the TV is tuned to that one flicker speed and ignores everything else. It is like being in a noisy classroom and still picking out your friend's voice, because you know exactly how it sounds.

The first TV remotes, around 1950, were plugged in with a long wire that people tripped over. In 1955 the American company Zenith sold the Flash-Matic, which an engineer named Eugene Polley designed. It shone a beam of visible light at sensors on the TV. On sunny days, sunlight could hit the sensors and change the channel.

The next year another Zenith engineer, Robert Adler, came up with the Space Command. Pressing a button made a tiny hammer strike an aluminium rod, which rang too high for humans to hear. The TV listened for each rod's note. The remote needed no batteries at all. It made a click as it worked, and many Americans still call a remote "the clicker". Infrared remotes took over in the late 1970s and 1980s.

Some newer remotes, especially for streaming boxes and smart TVs, don't use light at all. They talk to the TV with radio waves, often using [[@bluetooth|Bluetooth]], so you can press buttons with the remote under a cushion. Many also have a microphone, so you can just say the name of a show.

All of them still run on [[@batteries|batteries]], usually two small AAA or AA cells. A typical infrared remote uses so little power that a pair of batteries can last a year or more, because the LED is only on while a button is pressed. Remotes are also built to survive being dropped and sat on, which is why the buttons are soft rubber and the circuit board is sealed inside a tough plastic case.

text: A washing machine cleans clothes by doing four jobs at once. It soaks them in water. It adds detergent, a kind of soap that loosens dirt and grease. It moves the clothes around so they rub against each other and the water. And it gives all this enough time to work. Many machines also heat the water, because warm water helps [[dissolve|dissolve]] grease.
When washing is done, the machine drains the dirty water, rinses the clothes in clean water, and then spins them very fast to throw most of the water out.
People did the same things for thousands of years, scrubbing and beating clothes on stones by rivers. The machine just does the hard work for you.

st.prompt: In the spin cycle, the drum whirls round very fast. Where does the water go?

options.t: It's pushed to the middle of the drum and drains from there
It's flung outwards through holes in the drum wall
It turns into steam and disappears

st.reveal: As the drum spins, the clothes are pressed against its wall, but the water keeps trying to fly off in a straight line. It escapes through hundreds of small holes into the outer tub and is pumped away. A salad spinner works the same way.

d.try: Put a few drops of cooking oil in a jar of water, close the lid tightly and shake. The oil soon floats back up in blobs. Now add a drop of washing-up liquid and shake again. Watch how the oil breaks into tiny droplets that stay mixed in, just like grease leaving your clothes.
myth: The more detergent you use, the cleaner your clothes will be.
Extra detergent doesn't clean better. It can leave a sticky film on clothes, make too many suds and need extra rinsing. Following the amount on the packet works best.

one end grabs water, the other grabs grease

sec.t:
Water alone is not good at removing grease, because oil and water don't mix. Detergent solves this. Each detergent [[molecule|molecule]] is long and thin. One end loves water. The other end hates water but loves oil and grease.

When you wash, the oil-loving ends dig into greasy dirt, while the water-loving ends stick out into the water. Thousands of molecules surround each speck of grease, lift it off the cloth and keep it floating so it can be rinsed away. This is the same trick that makes [[@soap-germs|soap]] pull germs off your hands. Modern detergents also contain [[enzyme|enzymes]] that break down stains such as egg, blood and grass.

The two main kinds of machine move clothes differently. In a top-loader, you drop clothes in from above. A spinning post or disc at the bottom churns them round and round in deep water.

In a front-loader, the drum lies on its side like a rolling barrel. As it turns, paddles lift the clothes to the top, and they drop back down into a shallow pool of water. That tumbling, over and over, does the scrubbing. Front-loaders usually use less water and energy, though they take longer.

The rubbing matters. [[@friction|Friction]] between fibres and water knocks dirt loose, which is why a quick rinse with no movement leaves clothes still dirty.

{{story:mumbai}}

At the end, the drum spins very fast, often more than 1,000 times a minute in a front-loader. The clothes are pressed against the drum wall. The water, which tends to keep moving in a straight line, escapes through hundreds of small holes and is pumped away. Clothes come out damp, not dripping, so they dry much faster on the line.

Not everyone uses machines. At Mahalaxmi Dhobi Ghat in [[@mumbai|Mumbai]], an open-air laundry more than a hundred years old, hundreds of washers called dhobis still scrub and beat clothes in rows of concrete washing pens. Hotels and hospitals send them sheets by the sackful. Visitors watch from a bridge above.

In many homes across the world, washing is still done by hand, often by women and girls. The Swedish doctor Hans Rosling, in a famous talk in 2010, described the day his family got a washing machine. He said it gave his mother hours each week to read and to take him to the library. Some economists and historians argue that household machines like this changed women's lives as much as many laws did, freeing time for school and paid work.

The machine needs a lot of water and electricity, though. In places where water is scarce, a bucket and a scrubbing brush may still make more sense.

text: Behaving well online is mostly the same as behaving well anywhere: be kind, [[@truth-lies|be honest]] and think before you act. [[@internet-how|The internet]] just makes those choices travel faster and further.

A comment typed in a second can be screenshotted, shared and seen by thousands. A rumour forwarded without checking can cause real harm. A joke that seems funny in your head can hurt someone who can't see your smile.

People sometimes call this being a good digital citizen. It means protecting yourself, respecting others and checking things before you share them. Most of all, it means remembering there is a real person on the other side of the screen.

sec.t:
Face to face, you see someone's face fall when you say something unkind, and you often stop. Online, you don't. Psychologists call this the online disinhibition effect: people say things on screens they would never say in person.

Being anonymous, or thinking you are, makes it worse. So does speed. A good habit is to pause before posting anything when you are angry, and read it again later. Messages also lose your tone of voice. That is partly why [[@emojis|emojis]] became so popular, to show the feeling behind the words.

Everything you do online leaves traces: posts, photos, comments, searches and likes. Together they make your [[@digital-footprint|digital footprint]]. Some colleges and employers look at applicants' public posts.

Think about what you share about yourself, and about others. Posting a friend's photo or private message without asking can embarrass them. Keep personal details like your address, school and phone number private, and use strong [[@passwords|passwords]].

The internet also lets you do a lot of good. [[@wikipedia-how|Wikipedia]], the free online encyclopedia, is written mostly by volunteers who check each other's work. Young people have used online petitions and videos to raise money for causes and to share skills.

Small habits count too. Credit people when you share their drawing or photo. Say thank you when someone helps you in a game or forum. Disagree with ideas without attacking the person. Online spaces feel like the people in them, so each user shapes what everyone else sees.

[[@bullying|Bullying]] online, called [[@cyberbullying|cyberbullying]], can follow a child home, onto their phone, at any hour. If someone is cruel to you, don't reply in anger. Take a screenshot, block them and tell a trusted adult.

If you see someone else being bullied, a private kind message to them can mean a lot. In India, serious online crimes can be reported on the national helpline, 1930, or at the government's cybercrime website, with an adult's help.

Most social apps ask users to be at least 13, because of a 1998 American law called COPPA. It stops companies collecting personal data from younger children without a parent's permission. India's 2023 data protection law asks for a parent's consent for anyone under 18. Rules can protect you, but good habits protect you more, every time you pick up a phone.

text: Engineers solve practical problems using science and maths. A scientist might ask how something works. An engineer asks how to build something that works, safely, at a sensible cost and on time.

Civil engineers design roads, [[@bridges|bridges]], dams and buildings. Mechanical engineers design machines and engines. Electrical engineers work on power grids and [[circuit|circuits]]. Chemical engineers turn raw materials into fuels, medicines and plastics. Computer engineers design chips and software. And there are many more kinds, from engineers who design spacecraft to those who make sure clean water reaches every tap in a city.

sec.t:
Most engineering follows a loop. First, understand the problem: who needs what, where and with what limits? Then sketch ideas and pick the best ones. Next, calculate. How heavy will it be? How strong must it be? What happens in an earthquake or a storm?

Then test. Engineers build models, run computer simulations and break things on purpose in labs. Each test reveals weaknesses. They redesign and test again. Only after many rounds does the real thing get built. Even then, engineers keep inspecting it for years to check it is behaving as expected.

India celebrates Engineers' Day on 15 September, the birthday of M. Visvesvaraya, born in 1861 in a village in today's Karnataka. He designed automatic sluice gates to control water in [[reservoir|reservoirs]] and built flood protection for Hyderabad after a disastrous flood in 1908.

As chief engineer in the kingdom of Mysore, he led the building of the Krishna Raja Sagara dam near [[@mysuru|Mysuru]]. Its water irrigated huge areas of farmland and supplied the city. He was awarded the Bharat Ratna, India's highest civilian honour, in 1955, and lived to the age of 100.

sec.h: Emily Roebling and the Brooklyn Bridge
sec.t:
In New York, John Roebling designed the Brooklyn Bridge but died after an accident in 1869, before work began in earnest. His son Washington took over. In 1872 Washington became seriously ill after working in the pressurised chambers under the river, and could barely leave his room.

His wife, Emily Warren Roebling, stepped in. She studied mathematics, the strength of materials and cable construction, carried his instructions to the site and dealt with officials and engineers. When the bridge opened in 1883, she was the first person to cross it by carriage. A plaque on the bridge now honours her.

In India, engineering is one of the most popular university subjects, and the IITs and many state colleges train hundreds of thousands of engineers a year. In the USA, engineers usually study for four years and some take exams to become licensed professionals.

Good engineers are curious about how things work and stubborn about getting them right. They also have to think about people. A brilliant design for a [[@metro-trains|metro]] station is useless if passengers in wheelchairs cannot use it, or if it costs too much to build. The best engineering often disappears from view: you only notice the water, the power or the bridge when it fails.

text: A launch countdown is a timetable that runs backwards. Every job before a launch, from pumping in fuel to switching the rocket onto its own batteries, is given a time before zero. Teams call these times "T-minus": T-minus 2 hours, T-minus 10 minutes, T-minus 10 seconds. At T-zero, the engines light and the rocket lifts off. After that, the clock counts up: T-plus 1 minute, T-plus 2 minutes.

Counting backwards helps everyone see how much time is left. Big countdowns can last more than a day. They include planned pauses, called holds, when the clock stops while people check everything. The famous "10, 9, 8..." is only the very end.

st.reveal: Holds are built into the countdown on purpose. The clock stops at set points, such as T-minus 10 minutes, giving teams time to catch up, solve small problems and decide whether to go on. A countdown can sit in a hold for minutes or hours.

sec.t:
The countdown came from cinema. In 1929, the German director Fritz Lang made a silent film called *Frau im Mond*, or *Woman in the Moon*, about a rocket trip to the Moon. To build suspense before the launch, he showed numbers counting down on the screen: 10, 9, 8, down to "NOW".

Real rocket scientists worked as advisers on the film, and many saw it. When real rockets were built, from the 1940s onwards, engineers borrowed the idea. By the time of the space race in the 1950s and 1960s, countdowns had become part of every launch, broadcast on TV to millions.

Countdowns almost never run straight through. Holds are planned pauses. If launch is set for 3:00 pm, the clock might stop at T-minus 10 minutes for a while, so everything must be ready before the final push. That is why the T-minus time and the real time don't always match.

If something goes wrong, the team may call an unplanned hold. If it can't be fixed in time, they "scrub" the launch and try another day. Bad weather, a faulty valve or even a boat in the danger zone can scrub a launch.

In the last minutes, things happen too fast for people. Computers run the final sequence. On NASA's Space Shuttle, a computer took control at T-minus 31 seconds. If a [[sensor|sensor]] showed a problem, it could stop the launch in a fraction of a second, even after the engines had started.

At Sriharikota, ISRO also hands over the final minutes to an automatic launch sequence. For [[@chandrayaan|Chandrayaan-3]] in July 2023, the countdown began 25.5 hours before lift-off. In the final seconds, the computer checked every system again before the rocket's motors lit.

Counting down tells you how much time is left, which counting up can't do. That is useful for anything with a deadline. Microwaves and exam timers count down. So does the New Year clock at midnight and the big screens before a cricket match or the Olympics.

Countdowns also make people pay attention. In a crowd, the last ten numbers bring everyone together, shouting at once. Fritz Lang knew that in 1929. Today, when a rocket lifts off from Florida or [[@launch-sites|Sriharikota]], millions of people still count along, and the clock becomes one of the most exciting things in [[@science-fiction|science fiction]] that came true.

text: Animation in India is made the same way as anywhere else, with a mix of drawing, computer work and a great deal of patience. A team writes a story, sketches it as a comic-like storyboard and designs the characters. Then animators bring them to life frame by frame, either drawn by hand or built and moved inside a computer.

India has a large animation industry. Its studios make home-grown shows like *Chhota Bheem* and *Motu Patlu*, films based on myths and epics, and work for studios in the USA, Europe and Japan. Many of the artists working on cartoons watched by children in America sit in offices in Mumbai or Hyderabad.

sec.t:
Every animated film is an illusion. Your eye sees a quick series of still pictures and your brain blends them into smooth motion, the trick explained in [[@movies-move|how movies move]]. Films usually show 24 frames each second.

In traditional 2D animation, artists draw key poses first, such as the start and end of a jump. Then other artists draw the in-between pictures. In 3D animation, artists build a digital model of a character, give it a skeleton of joints, a step called rigging, and move it pose by pose on a computer. Lighting and shading are added, and powerful computers "render" each finished frame. A single frame of a detailed film can take hours to render.

The big change came in the 2000s, when cable channels needed lots of children's shows. In 2005, the animated film *Hanuman* became a surprise hit in cinemas. In 2008, a Hyderabad studio called Green Gold Animation launched *Chhota Bheem*, about a strong, kind boy in the village of Dholakpur. It became one of the most popular children's shows in India.

Other characters followed, like *Motu Patlu*, based on an old comic, and *Little Singham*. These shows were cheaper to make than many foreign cartoons and spoke directly to Indian children, with laddoos, festivals and village life.

Indian studios also do a lot of work for others. They might animate scenes, add [[@special-effects|visual effects]], paint backgrounds or clean up 3D models for films made in Hollywood or Europe. Some Indian-owned effects companies have worked on films that won Oscars for visual effects.

The government calls this the AVGC sector, short for animation, visual effects, gaming and comics, and has set up training programmes because the industry needs more skilled artists.

For years, Indian animated films struggled in cinemas, where big Hollywood cartoons won most of the audience. Then, in July 2025, *Mahavatar Narsimha*, a 3D film about Vishnu's half-lion, half-man avatar, opened with little fanfare and kept growing by word of mouth. It earned around ₹300 crore or more, far more than any Indian animated film before.

Its success persuaded many producers that Indian audiences will pay for home-made animation. Studios are now working on more feature films, often drawing on the [[@ramayana|Ramayana]], the Mahabharata and folk tales, and on new stories too.

text: हर किसी का [[@blood|खून]] लाल होता है, पर हर किसी का खून एक जैसा नहीं होता। हर लाल रक्त कोशिका की सतह पर शक्कर और [[protein|प्रोटीन]] से बने नन्हे निशान होते हैं। वैज्ञानिक इन्हें [[antigen|एंटीजन]] कहते हैं। तुम्हारी कोशिकाओं पर कौन-से निशान हैं, इसी से तुम्हारा ब्लड ग्रुप तय होता है।

मुख्य व्यवस्था में चार ग्रुप हैं। ग्रुप A की कोशिकाओं पर A निशान होता है, ग्रुप B पर B निशान, ग्रुप AB पर दोनों, और ग्रुप O पर कोई भी नहीं। एक दूसरा निशान, जिसे आरएच कहते हैं, या तो होता है (पॉज़िटिव) या नहीं होता (नेगेटिव)। तो कोई A पॉज़िटिव हो सकता है, तो कोई O नेगेटिव।
जब एक व्यक्ति का खून दूसरे को चढ़ाया जाता है, तब ये निशान बहुत मायने रखते हैं। गलत ग्रुप का खून चढ़ जाए, तो शरीर की सुरक्षा सेना नए खून पर हमला कर सकती है।

अगर उस व्यक्ति को ग्रुप B का खून चढ़ा दिया जाए, तो एंटीबॉडी नई कोशिकाओं को पकड़कर उन्हें गुच्छों में चिपका देती हैं, जिससे मरीज़ की हालत बहुत बिगड़ सकती है। इसलिए खून चढ़ाने से पहले [[@hospitals|अस्पताल]] हमेशा मरीज़ और दान किए गए खून, दोनों की जाँच करते हैं। O नेगेटिव लाल कोशिकाओं पर न A निशान होता है, न B, न आरएच। इसलिए इमरजेंसी में ये लगभग हर किसी को चल जाती हैं।

1952 में डॉ. वाई.एम. भेंडे और उनके साथियों को [[@mumbai|मुंबई]] में, जिसे तब बॉम्बे कहते थे, ऐसा खून मिला जो किसी खाने में फ़िट नहीं बैठता था। आम जाँच में यह ग्रुप O जैसा दिखता था, फिर भी साधारण O खून के साथ इसमें गुच्छे बन जाते थे। इन लोगों में H नाम का एक बुनियादी निशान नहीं था, जो लगभग हर किसी में होता है।

बॉम्बे ग्रुप वाले लोग सिर्फ़ दूसरे बॉम्बे दानदाताओं से ही खून ले सकते हैं। भारत में यह लगभग 10,000 में से 1 व्यक्ति में मिलता है, और यूरोप में लगभग दस लाख में से 1 में। भारत के ब्लड बैंक बॉम्बे ग्रुप वाले दानदाताओं की सूचियाँ रखते हैं, ताकि इमरजेंसी में उन्हें बुलाया जा सके।

तुम्हें अपना ब्लड ग्रुप माता-पिता से, अपने [[@genes-family|जीन]] के ज़रिए मिलता है। हर माता या पिता A, B या O में से एक रूप आगे देता है। ग्रुप A वाले दो माता-पिता का बच्चा भी ग्रुप O का हो सकता है, अगर दोनों अपने भीतर छिपा O आगे दे दें।

दुनिया भर में ग्रुप अलग-अलग ढंग से फैले हैं। अमेरिका में O पॉज़िटिव सबसे आम है। भारत में B और O दोनों बहुत आम हैं, और ग्रुप B यूरोप के मुकाबले कहीं ज़्यादा मिलता है। आरएच नेगेटिव खून भारत में अमेरिका से कम मिलता है।

sec.h: जानवरों के भी ब्लड ग्रुप होते हैं
sec.t: [[@dogs-domestic|कुत्तों]] के अपने कम से कम दर्जन भर ब्लड ग्रुप होते हैं। बिल्लियों के तीन मुख्य ग्रुप हैं, A, B और AB। [[@jobs-vet|जानवरों के डॉक्टर]] [[@life-pets-world|पालतू जानवरों]] के लिए वैसे ही खून का मिलान करते हैं जैसे अस्पताल इंसानों के लिए। कुछ शहरों में तो कुत्तों के ब्लड बैंक भी हैं।

खून किसी कारखाने में नहीं बन सकता, इसलिए हर बार खून चढ़ाना किसी दानदाता पर टिका होता है। दुर्घटना के बाद के मरीज़, मुश्किल प्रसव से गुज़रती माँएँ, और थैलेसीमिया जैसी खून की बीमारी वाले बच्चे, इन सबको बार-बार खून की ज़रूरत पड़ सकती है। अपना ब्लड ग्रुप जानना काम की बात है। और जब तुम बड़े हो जाओ, तो खून दान करना किसी अनजान की मदद का सबसे आसान तरीका है।

text: तुम्हारे दिमाग में गहरे बैठा है हाइपोथैलेमस, जो लगभग एक बादाम जितना बड़ा हिस्सा है। यह एसी के थर्मोस्टैट की तरह काम करता है और शरीर को लगभग 37 °C पर रखता है।

जब तुम्हारा [[@immune-system|प्रतिरक्षा तंत्र]] कीटाणुओं से लड़ रहा होता है, तो वह कुछ रासायनिक संदेश छोड़ता है जो हाइपोथैलेमस तक पहुँचते हैं। ये संदेश उससे कहते हैं कि सेटिंग एक-दो डिग्री बढ़ा दो। फिर शरीर खुद को गर्म करने में जुट जाता है, और तापमान की यही बढ़त बुखार है। बहुत-से [[germ|कीटाणु]] ज़्यादा गर्मी में धीरे बढ़ते हैं, और तुम्हारी कुछ प्रतिरक्षा कोशिकाएँ तेज़ी से काम करती हैं। इसलिए बुखार आम तौर पर इस बात का [[symptom|लक्षण]] है कि शरीर लड़ रहा है, न कि यह कि लड़ाई में कुछ गड़बड़ हो गई है।

sec.t:
बुखार अक्सर कई चरणों में आता है। पहले [[@brain-works|दिमाग]] की नई सेटिंग शरीर के तापमान से ऊँची होती है, इसलिए तुम्हें ठंड लगती है। त्वचा की खून की नलियाँ सिकुड़ जाती हैं ताकि गर्मी अंदर बची रहे, और इससे तुम पीले दिख सकते हो। मांसपेशियाँ झटकों में तेज़ी से काँपती हैं, यही कँपकँपी है। कँपकँपी से गर्मी बनती है, वैसे ही जैसे सर्दियों में हथेलियाँ रगड़ने से।

जब शरीर नई सेटिंग तक पहुँच जाता है, तो तुम्हें गर्मी लग सकती है और चेहरा तमतमा सकता है। बीमारी कम होने पर सेटिंग वापस सामान्य पर आ जाती है। अब शरीर सेटिंग से ज़्यादा गर्म है, इसलिए तुम्हें [[@sweat|पसीना]] आता है और तुम चादर फेंक देते हो। इसे ही बुखार उतरना कहते हैं।

ज़्यादातर इतिहास में डॉक्टर माथा छूकर बुखार का अंदाज़ा लगाते थे, जैसे आज भी घर में माँ करती हैं। 1600 के दशक की शुरुआत में सैंतोरियो सैंतोरियो नाम के एक इतालवी डॉक्टर ने शरीर की गर्मी नापने वाले पहले यंत्रों में से एक बनाया। शुरुआती डॉक्टरी [[@thermometer|थर्मामीटर]] लगभग 30 सेंटीमीटर लंबे होते थे और रीडिंग देने में 20 मिनट तक लगा देते थे।

आज भारत और दुनिया के ज़्यादातर हिस्सों में शरीर का तापमान सेल्सियस में नापा जाता है। अमेरिका में यह आम तौर पर फ़ारेनहाइट में होता है, जहाँ सामान्य तापमान लगभग 98.6 °F है और बुखार लगभग 100.4 °F से शुरू होता है। दोनों [[@temperature-scales|पैमाने]] एक ही गर्मी को अलग-अलग सीढ़ियों में नापते हैं।

sec.h: कब किसी बड़े को बताना है
sec.t:
बच्चों में ज़्यादातर बुखार [[@cold-flu|सर्दी-ज़ुकाम]] जैसे आम संक्रमणों से होते हैं और कुछ दिनों में उतर जाते हैं। आराम करना और खूब पानी पीना मदद करता है। कुछ दवाइयाँ बुखार उतारकर आराम दे सकती हैं, पर इनके बारे में फ़ैसला सिर्फ़ कोई बड़ा ही करे।

डॉक्टर ज़रूर जानना चाहते हैं अगर किसी नन्हे शिशु को बुखार हो, बहुत तेज़ बुखार हो, या बुखार कुछ दिनों से ज़्यादा टिक जाए। वे यह भी जानना चाहते हैं अगर बुखार के साथ गर्दन अकड़ी हो, ऐसे दाने हों जो दबाने पर फीके न पड़ें, या साँस लेने में दिक्कत हो। तबीयत ठीक न लगे, तो माँ-बाप, टीचर या डॉक्टर को बताना हमेशा सही पहला कदम है।

text: सुश्रुत वह नाम है जो दुनिया में सर्जरी की सबसे पुरानी किताबों में से एक, *सुश्रुत संहिता* (सुश्रुत का संग्रह), से जुड़ा है। यह [[@sanskrit|संस्कृत]] में लिखी गई थी और भारत की पारंपरिक चिकित्सा, [[@ayurveda-yoga|आयुर्वेद]], के बुनियादी ग्रंथों में से एक है।

परंपरा कहती है कि सुश्रुत एक [[surgeon|सर्जन]] थे, जिन्होंने काशी में एक गुरु से शिक्षा पाई। काशी को आज [[@varanasi|वाराणसी]] कहते हैं। इस किताब में लगभग 300 ऑपरेशनों और 100 से ज़्यादा औज़ारों का वर्णन है। इसमें टूटी [[@bones|हड्डियाँ]] बैठाने, आँख से धुँधला [[lens|लेंस]] हटाने, घाव सिलने और, सबसे मशहूर, कटी हुई नाक फिर से बनाने की बातें हैं।
सुश्रुत असल में कौन थे, और ठीक-ठीक कब रहे, यह कोई नहीं जानता। जो बचा है, वह किताब है।

तरबूज़, चमड़े की थैलियाँ और अभ्यास
sec.t:
संहिता ट्रेनिंग को लेकर बहुत सख़्त है। छात्र को ग्रंथ भी पढ़ने होते थे, और देखकर अभ्यास भी करना होता था। चीरे का अभ्यास लौकी, खीरे और ख़रबूज़े पर होता था। छेद करने का अभ्यास पानी या कीचड़ से भरी चमड़े की थैलियों पर। टाँके कपड़े और नरम चमड़े पर लगाकर देखे जाते थे। खोखले तनों पर छात्र नली डालकर टटोलना सीखते थे।

इसमें औज़ारों की सूची भी है, जिनमें से बहुत-से जानवरों और चिड़ियों की चोंच या जबड़ों के आकार के हैं। साथ ही यह भी बताया गया है कि इन्हें धारदार और साफ़ कैसे रखें।

प्राचीन भारत में कभी-कभी किसी की नाक काट देना एक क्रूर सज़ा के रूप में इस्तेमाल होता था। इसलिए नाक फिर से बनाने के तरीके की माँग थी। संहिता बताती है कि गाल से ज़िंदा [[@skin|त्वचा]] का एक टुकड़ा काटो, उसे जुड़ा रहने देते हुए घुमाकर लाओ, और नाक के ऊपर आकार दो। नथुने खुले रखने के लिए दो छोटी नलियाँ लगाई जाती थीं।

समय के साथ भारतीय वैद्य गाल के बजाय माथे की त्वचा इस्तेमाल करने लगे। 1794 में लंदन की *जेंटलमैन्स मैगज़ीन* ने पुणे के पास एक आदमी पर किए गए इसी ऑपरेशन की रिपोर्ट छापी। यूरोप के सर्जनों ने इसकी नकल की, और यह "भारतीय तरीके" के नाम से मशहूर हो गया। प्लास्टिक सर्जन आज भी माथे की त्वचा वाला यह तरीका इस्तेमाल करते हैं।

संहिता में नाक से कहीं ज़्यादा बातें हैं। इसमें मोतियाबिंद के इलाज का एक तरीका बताया गया है। मोतियाबिंद में आँख के अंदर का लेंस धुँधला हो जाता है, और [[pupil|पुतली]] के पीछे सफ़ेदी-सी दिखने लगती है। एक बारीक सुई से धुँधले लेंस को देखने के रास्ते से हटा दिया जाता था। इस तरीके को कूचिंग कहते हैं, और सदियों तक दुनिया के कई हिस्सों में यह इस्तेमाल होता रहा।

किताब यह भी समझाती है कि खपच्चियों से टूटी हड्डियाँ कैसे बैठाएँ और शरीर में धँसे तीर कैसे निकालें। इसमें पौधों और खनिजों से बनी सैकड़ों दवाओं की सूची है।

sec.h: दुनिया के वैद्यों के बीच सुश्रुत
sec.t:
मिस्र से यूनान और चीन तक, बहुत-सी प्राचीन सभ्यताओं में कुशल वैद्य थे। उनके बारे में तुम [[@doctors-history|डॉक्टरों के इतिहास]] में पढ़ सकते हो। सुश्रुत की किताब इस बात में अलग दिखती है कि यह कितनी व्यावहारिक है। इसे पढ़कर लगता है जैसे किसी काम करते सर्जन की गाइड हो।

इसकी हर बात आज के विज्ञान से मेल नहीं खाती। यह बीमारी को शरीर के संतुलन के बारे में आयुर्वेद के विचारों से समझाती है, और इसके कुछ इलाज अब इस्तेमाल नहीं होंगे। पर ट्रेनिंग, साफ़-सफ़ाई और सावधानी से [[@scabs|घाव भरने]] पर इसका ध्यान आज भी डॉक्टरों को प्रभावित करता है।

काशी से बहुत दूर, ऑस्ट्रेलिया के मेलबर्न में रॉयल ऑस्ट्रेलेशियन कॉलेज ऑफ़ सर्जन्स में सुश्रुत की एक मूर्ति खड़ी है। यह इस बात का निशान है कि दुनिया भर के सर्जन उनका नाम कितना जानते हैं।

text: Plenty of everyday things began in the head of a child. The ice lolly, earmuffs, the trampoline, an early snowmobile and the braille alphabet were all dreamed up by kids aged about 11 to 16.

Kids notice problems that grown-ups have stopped seeing. Cold ears, slow reading, a boring winter. They also aren't afraid to try silly-looking ideas. Some of those ideas went on to change millions of lives, and a few became famous brands.

st.reveal: Braille went blind at age 3 and was a student at a school for blind children in Paris when he made his system around 1824. He was about 15.

sec.t:
Louis Braille was born in France in 1809. At age 3 he hurt his eye with a sharp tool in his father's workshop, and an [[infection|infection]] left him blind in both eyes. At school in Paris, blind students read books with huge raised letters. They were heavy and painfully slow.

A French army captain had invented "night writing", a code of raised dots so soldiers could read in the dark. It used 12 dots and was clumsy. Young Louis cut it down to just six dots in a small grid, enough for every letter, number and punctuation mark. He was about 15. Today [[@braille|braille]] is read by millions of blind people in dozens of languages, including Hindi and Tamil.

In 1873, Chester Greenwood, 15, from Maine in the USA, kept getting freezing ears while ice skating. He bent some wire into loops and asked his grandmother to sew fur onto them. Earmuffs. He patented an improved version in 1877, and his hometown still holds a Chester Greenwood Day parade.

George Nissen, 16, of Iowa, watched trapeze artists drop into safety nets and bounce. In 1930 he started building a frame with stretched canvas so he could keep bouncing. He later made his name with the word "trampoline", from the Spanish word for diving board. Today the [[@how-trampoline|trampoline]] is even an Olympic sport.

In Canada, Joseph-Armand Bombardier was 15 in 1922 when he built a snow machine with a car engine and a [[propeller|propeller]]. His later inventions led to the snowmobile and the giant Bombardier company, which went on to build trains and planes.

Children still invent. In 2020, Gitanjali Rao, a 15-year-old from Colorado, was named TIME magazine's first Kid of the Year. She had designed a device to test for lead in drinking water, using a [[sensor|sensor]] and a phone app. In India, school science fairs and programmes such as the Dr. A.P.J. Abdul Kalam IGNITE awards have honoured children's ideas for farm tools, safer roads and helping elderly people.

Some kid patents are less serious. In 2002, a five-year-old in the United States was granted a patent for a new way of swinging on a swing, sideways. His father, a patent lawyer, filed it to teach him how patents work. It joins a long list of [[@inventions-weird|weird inventions]] that got official approval.

text: For hundreds of thousands of years, people lived by hunting and gathering. Then, starting around 11,500 years ago, some groups in the Middle East began to plant seeds of wild grasses and keep herds of [[@goats-sheep|goats and sheep]]. Over many generations, they chose the best plants and the calmest animals, and those slowly changed. This is called domestication.

Farming was not invented once. It began in at least half a dozen regions, at different times, with different crops. Within a few thousand years, farmers had settled villages, food stores and far more children than hunters could feed. That set the stage for towns and cities.

st.prompt: Teosinte is the wild grass that farmers in Mexico slowly turned into maize. How big were its seed heads?

options.t: About as long as your thumb, with a few hard seeds
Bigger than a modern corn cob
About the same as today's corn

st.reveal: A teosinte ear is only a few centimetres long, with around a dozen seeds locked in hard cases. Over thousands of years, farmers kept seeds from the plants with the biggest, softest ears. Step by step, they made the corn cob.

src: Encyclopaedia Britannica, origins of agriculture.
Smithsonian Institution, National Museum of Natural History, "Agriculture" in Human Origins.
Diamond J. (1997) Guns, Germs, and Steel.
n.certNote: Archaeologists agree farming began around 12,000 to 10,000 years ago in several places. They still debate exactly why it started, and the dates for some crops and regions.

d.try: Soak a few dried moong or chana in water overnight, then place them on wet cotton in a saucer near a window. Keep them damp and check every day. Pick the strongest sprouts and plant them in a pot of soil. You are doing what the first farmers did, choosing which plants get to grow.
myth: Farming was invented in one place and spread from there to the rest of the world.

Farming began independently in several regions, each with its own local plants and animals. Wheat and goats came from the Middle East, rice and millet from China, maize and beans from Mexico, potatoes from the Andes.
facts: about 11,500 years ago, in the Fertile Crescent (Middle East)
first grown in Mexico about 9,000 years ago
first grown in China, in the Yangtze River valley

sec.t:
The first known farmers lived in an arc of land from today's Israel and Jordan, up through Syria and Turkey and down to Iraq and Iran. Historians call it the Fertile Crescent. Here grew wild [[@wheat-bread|wheat]], barley, lentils and peas.

Wild wheat has a problem for people: when ripe, the seeds fall off and scatter. A few plants, by chance, held on to their seeds. When people harvested with sickles, those were the ones they carried home and planted. Over time, fields filled with wheat that waited to be picked.

Animals changed too. Goats and sheep were tamed here, and cattle soon after. Dogs had joined people even earlier, while everyone was still hunting. Taming an animal took many generations of keeping the gentlest ones and letting them breed, until the herd behaved very differently from its wild cousins.

Farming is hard work. So why did people choose it? Nobody knows for sure. As the last ice age ended, the [[climate|climate]] grew warmer and wetter, and wild grains became plentiful in some places. People may have settled near these grains, grown in number, and then needed to plant more to feed everyone.

Some groups built big stone monuments before they farmed. At [[@mystery-gobekli|Göbekli Tepe]] in Turkey, people carved huge stone pillars about 11,000 years ago. Gatherings at such places may have needed a lot of food, which could have pushed people to grow it.

Farming fed more people, but life was not always better. Skeletons show that many early farmers were shorter than hunters before them, and had more tooth decay and disease. Living close to animals and to each other spread germs. A failed harvest could mean [[famine|famine]].

The writer Jared Diamond once called farming "the worst mistake in the history of the human race". Many historians disagree, pointing to what farming made possible: food stores, trades, writing and [[@first-cities|cities]]. Today about 8 billion people depend on the crops those first farmers chose, grown on fields that still need good soil and steady rain.

text: The first motor car in India is usually said to have arrived in Calcutta in 1897, owned by a British resident. A year later, in 1898, four cars appeared on the streets of Bombay. One belonged to the industrialist Jamsetji Tata.

These early cars were imported from Europe, noisy and slow, with top speeds around 30 km/h, a bit faster than a good cyclist. Roads were made for bullock carts and horse carriages, so a car journey often involved punctures, breakdowns and a crowd of curious onlookers.

st.prompt: India's first steam car was built in 1903. Where?

options.t: Madras
Delhi
Lahore

st.reveal: Samuel John Green, an engineer at a Madras coachbuilding firm, built a steam-powered car there in 1903. Madras also gave its early cars registration numbers starting with MC.

src: Business Standard, "The first wheels roll into India" (2008).
Maruti Suzuki India, company history.
n.certNote: Early records are patchy. Most histories say the first car reached Calcutta in 1897 and four reached Bombay in 1898, but the owners and makes of the very first cars are not well documented.

d.try: Make a "car through time" chart. Ask the oldest person you know what car their family had first, and when. Then ask your parents. Add your own family's car today, or a bus or scooter if you don't have a car. Compare how the vehicles changed.
myth: The Ambassador was an Indian design.
It was based on the British Morris Oxford of the 1950s. Hindustan Motors built it in India with Indian parts for 56 years, and it became so common that many people thought of it as India's own.
facts: New passenger vehicles sold in India

sec.t:
The world's first practical petrol car, built by Karl Benz in Germany, appeared in 1886. Just over ten years later, rich Indians and British officials were importing [[@cars-history|cars]] by ship.

They looked like carriages with the horse removed. Drivers sat high up, steered with a [[lever|lever]] or wheel, and wore goggles against the dust. There were no petrol pumps. Fuel came in tins, bought from chemists or hardware shops. A horse could take fright at the clatter, so some towns made rules about speed and noise.

Cars also needed numbers. Bombay and Madras began registering motor vehicles in the early 1900s, and each car got a plate with letters for its city. Madras cars carried "MC" numbers, and the first registered car in the south, MC-1, belonged to a railway official named Francis Spring. Driving licences followed, though early tests were simple. Most owners hired a trained driver, called a chauffeur, who also cleaned and repaired the car.

In Madras, a director of Parry and Company drove his car daily from Adyar to his office from 1901. In 1903, the engineer Samuel John Green built India's first steam car in the same city.

{{story:cars-engine}}

The keenest early buyers were India's princes. Maharajas ordered Rolls-Royces, Daimlers and Bentleys, sometimes dozens at a time, often with custom bodies covered in silver, ivory or brocade. Some were built as hunting cars, with seats for spotting tigers.

By the 1930s, Indian princes were among the biggest customers of Rolls-Royce anywhere outside Britain. Some of those cars still survive and appear at vintage car shows in Mumbai, Delhi and Gujarat, polished and still running.

One of the best known is a 1920s Rolls-Royce built for a maharaja's hunting trips, with a searchlight for spotting animals at night. Collectors in India now restore such cars piece by piece, sometimes hunting for years for one missing part.

After independence in 1947, India wanted to build its own cars. Hindustan Motors, near [[@kolkata|Kolkata]], began making the Ambassador in 1958, based on a British design. Premier made the Padmini in Bombay, based on an Italian Fiat.

For decades, these two were almost the only choices. Families waited months or even years to buy one. The rounded white Ambassador became the official car of ministers, and the black-and-yellow Padmini became Mumbai's famous taxi, until it was retired in 2023.

sec.h: The little car that changed everything
sec.t:
On 14 December 1983, Prime Minister Indira Gandhi handed the keys of the first Maruti 800 to Harpal Singh, a Delhi airline employee. The small, fuel-saving car, made with the Japanese company Suzuki, cost about Rs 50,000. For millions of middle-class families, it was their first car. The Maruti 800 stayed on sale for about 30 years, until 2014, and close to 29 lakh were sold. Many are still chugging along on Indian roads.

Today India is the world's third-largest market for new cars, behind China and the USA, selling about 43 lakh passenger vehicles in 2024–25. And the next big change has already started, as more Indian buyers switch to [[@electric-cars|electric cars]]. Surprisingly, electric cars are older than petrol ones. Some of the first motor vehicles of the 1880s ran on batteries.

text: The ancient Olympics, held at Olympia in Greece for more than a thousand years, had some events that would look very odd today. There was a race in armour, a fighting sport with almost no rules, a mule-cart race, and contests for trumpeters and heralds. Athletes competed without clothes, and the long jump was done holding stone or metal weights.

The Games were part of a religious festival for Zeus, king of the gods in [[@greek-myths|Greek myths]]. Winners got only a wreath of olive leaves. It was cut with a golden knife from a sacred wild olive tree growing near the temple of Zeus. Their home cities, though, often gave them free meals for life, statues and fame.

st.prompt: In 396 BC, a Spartan woman named Kyniska became an Olympic champion. How, if women were not allowed to compete?

options.t: She owned the winning chariot horses
She disguised herself as a man
She won the women's running race

st.reveal: In chariot racing, the prize went to the owner of the horses, not the driver. Kyniska bred and trained winning horses and took the olive wreath twice, in 396 and 392 BC, without ever setting foot on the track.

src: Pausanias, Description of Greece, Book V.
Judith Swaddling, The Ancient Olympic Games (British Museum Press).
n.certNote: Much of what we know comes from writers like Pausanias, who lived centuries after many of the events. The traditional start date of 776 BC and the end around AD 393 are both debated.

d.try: Hold your own "halteres" long jump. Stand with feet together and do a standing jump. Then try again holding a small water bottle in each hand, swinging your arms forward as you jump. Measure both with a tape. Did the swing help?
myth: The ancient Olympics stopped all wars in Greece while they were on.
A sacred truce protected athletes and visitors travelling to and from Olympia. It did not end wars between Greek cities, which often kept fighting elsewhere.
facts: Contests for trumpeters and heralds added

sec.t:
According to tradition, the first Games in 776 BC had just one event, the *stadion*. It was a sprint of one length of the stadium, about 192 m, roughly twice the length of a modern 100 m track race. Runners started from stone lines set into the ground, with grooves for their toes. Some of these starting lines can still be seen at Olympia today, and visitors like to race each other along the old track. A cook named Koroibos is listed as the first winner.

Over the next 200 years, more events were added: longer runs, wrestling, boxing, chariot races and the pentathlon. At its peak, the festival lasted five days, and tens of thousands of visitors camped around [[@ancient-olympia|Olympia]].

The *pankration* mixed boxing and wrestling. Kicking, punching, joint locks and choke holds were all allowed. The only rules were no biting and no gouging eyes. A fight carried on until one man gave up by raising a finger.

Greek boxers had no rounds and no weight classes. They wrapped their hands in leather straps instead of gloves. Indian wrestlers in old [[@wrestling-india|akharas]] trained hard too, but most of their bouts used far stricter rules than the pankration.

sec.h: Strange events that came and went
sec.t:
From 500 BC, there was a race for carts pulled by mules. It was dropped after about 56 years, perhaps because people found it boring or undignified. Another event, for mares, came and went at about the same time.

In 396 BC, contests for trumpeters and heralds were added. They were judged on how loud and clear they were. The winners then got the job of announcing the other events. One trumpeter, Herodoros of Megara, is said to have won ten times in a row.

In AD 67, the Roman emperor Nero came to compete. The Games were even moved by two years to fit his travel plans. He entered a chariot race with ten horses, fell out of his chariot, and failed to finish. The judges still crowned him champion.

After Nero's death, his win was struck from the official list. The Games carried on until around AD 393. When they were revived in Athens in 1896, the organisers kept the running, wrestling and discus, and left out the mule carts and trumpeters. Some unusual sports did survive into modern times, and a few are listed among today's [[@sport-weird|weirdest sports]].

text: The USA has had 47 presidencies since 1789, held by 45 people. Behind the official portraits are some odd and human stories. One president was a champion wrestler. One first lady raised silkworms in the White House. Two founders died on the same day, the country's 50th birthday.
Presidents have been tall and short, rich and poor, young and old. Their stories show that the job has changed hugely, from horses and handwritten letters to jets, television and phones.

st.prompt: George Washington had very bad teeth and wore dentures. What were they made of?

options.t: Ivory, metal and human and animal teeth
Wood
Glass

st.reveal: Washington's false teeth were made from hippopotamus ivory, metal springs and real teeth, some from animals and some from people. The story of wooden teeth is a myth.

d.try: Make a "presidents surprise quiz" for your family. Write ten facts from this article on slips of paper, but change three of them so they are false. See who can spot the fakes.
myth: George Washington had wooden false teeth.
None of his dentures were wooden. They used ivory, metal and real teeth. Over time they may have stained and cracked, which could have made them look like wood grain.
facts: Only presidents with two non-back-to-back terms
First president to live in the White House

sec.t:
George Washington was the first president, but he never lived in the White House. It was not finished until 1800, and John Adams moved in first. Washington also never lived in Washington, DC, the capital named after him. The White House was not even officially called that until 1901, when Theodore Roosevelt made the name official.

Grover Cleveland was the 22nd and the 24th president, with someone else in between. For more than a century he was the only one to serve two terms that were not back to back. Then Donald Trump, the 45th president, returned as the 47th in 2025. So the numbers keep running ahead of the people.

Thomas Jefferson and John Adams were close friends, then bitter rivals, then friends again through letters in old age. Both died on 4 July 1826, exactly 50 years after the Declaration of Independence that both had helped create. Adams' last words are said to have been "Thomas Jefferson survives", though Jefferson had died a few hours earlier. A fifth president, James Monroe, also died on 4 July, five years later.

William Henry Harrison gave the longest inauguration speech in history in 1841, nearly two hours in cold weather. He fell ill and died 31 days later, the shortest presidency ever. Doctors at the time blamed a cold. Many modern experts suspect a disease from dirty drinking water.

Theodore Roosevelt's family kept a zoo of pets at the White House, including snakes, a badger and a pony that once rode the lift upstairs. On a hunting trip in 1902, Roosevelt refused to shoot a bear that had been tied to a tree. A cartoon about it inspired toymakers to sell "Teddy's bear", the first [[@pop-teddy-bear|teddy bear]].

Later presidents brought dogs, cats, birds and once a raccoon. Calvin Coolidge was given the raccoon to eat for a Thanksgiving dinner. He kept it as a pet instead and named it Rebecca.

Four presidents, Washington, Jefferson, Theodore Roosevelt and Lincoln, are carved 18 metres high on [[@mount-rushmore|Mount Rushmore]]. The carving took 14 years and around 400 workers, and none of them died on the job. [[@george-washington|Washington]] was the first face finished. How a country with no king learned to pick a leader every four years is a stranger story still, told in [[@elections-usa|US elections]].

text: The Alhambra is a hilltop palace and [[fortress|fortress]] in Granada, a city in southern Spain. Its name comes from the Arabic *al-hamra*, "the red one", after the reddish clay of its outer walls. From outside, it looks like a plain, tough castle.

Inside is a different world of courtyards, pools, fountains and rooms covered in carved plaster and coloured tiles. Most of it was built in the 1300s by the Nasrid sultans, the last Muslim rulers in Spain. Today it is one of the most visited monuments in Europe, and tickets often sell out weeks ahead.
