d.try: Cut a square from card and snip a shape out of one side. Tape that piece onto the opposite side. Trace around your new shape again and again on paper, fitting each copy against the last. You'll end up with a tiling pattern that leaves no gaps, the same idea used in the Alhambra's tiles.
myth: The Alhambra was built all at once by one ruler.
It grew over hundreds of years. There was a fort on the hill by the 800s, the main palaces went up in the 1300s, and Christian rulers added a large Renaissance palace in the 1500s.
facts: Name means "the red one" in Arabic, after the colour of its walls

sec.t:
For nearly 800 years, from 711, much of what is now Spain and Portugal was ruled by Muslim kings. They called the land al-Andalus. Its cities were known for their libraries, scholars, poets and gardens. Muslims, Christians and Jews often lived side by side there, though not always peacefully.

Over the centuries, Christian kingdoms in the north pushed south. By the 1200s, only the kingdom of Granada was left. The Nasrid family ruled it for more than 250 years, and they built the Alhambra as their palace, government centre and fortress all at once.

Look closely at almost any wall in the Alhambra and you'll find writing. Bands of Arabic [[@calligraphy-world|calligraphy]] run across the plaster. One phrase, "There is no victor but God", appears thousands of times. There are also long poems, written for the rooms by court poets such as Ibn Zamrak.

Islamic art in religious and royal buildings often avoided pictures of people, so artists turned to [[geometry|geometry]]. The Alhambra's tiles fit together in patterns with no gaps, called [[@tessellations|tessellations]]. Ceilings are covered in muqarnas, thousands of tiny carved pieces that look like honeycomb or icicles.

In 1492, after a long siege, the last sultan of Granada, Muhammad XII, known in Spain as Boabdil, handed over the city to Queen Isabella and King Ferdinand. A Spanish legend says he looked back at the Alhambra and wept. The spot is still called "the Moor's last sigh".

The same year, the new rulers forced Jews to convert or leave Spain. Muslims were later forced to convert too. Isabella and Ferdinand also agreed to fund a sailor named [[@columbus|Christopher Columbus]], who set off across the Atlantic that August.

Over the next centuries the Alhambra fell into neglect. In 1829, the American writer Washington Irving stayed in its empty rooms. His book *Tales of the Alhambra* (1832) made it famous in the US and Europe, and visitors began to arrive.

In 1922, and again in 1936, a young Dutch artist named M. C. Escher sketched the tiles. Their patterns pushed him to create his famous tilings of birds, fish and lizards. A palace built for sultans ended up changing modern art and inspiring maths teachers around the world.

text: The Victoria Memorial is a huge white marble building in [[@kolkata|Kolkata]], set in about 26 hectares of gardens and ponds. It was built between 1906 and 1921 to remember Queen Victoria of Britain, who had been Empress of India until she died in 1901.

It was never a palace or a home. From the start it was meant to be a memorial and a [[@museums|museum]] of British rule in India. Today it holds paintings, maps, coins, weapons and documents, and it's one of the most visited places in the city.
On winter evenings, families picnic on its lawns and children feed the fish in its ponds, much as they did a hundred years ago.

st.prompt: The Victoria Memorial was built for Queen Victoria. How many times did she visit India?

options.t: Never
Once, for her coronation as Empress
Every winter

st.reveal: Queen Victoria became Empress of India in 1877 but never travelled there. She ruled from Britain and learned Hindustani from an Indian attendant, Abdul Karim, instead.

myth: The Victoria Memorial was Queen Victoria's palace in India.
She never visited India, and nobody ever lived there. It was built after her death as a memorial and museum, and it still works as a museum today.
facts: donations from princes, officials and the public

sec.t:
When Victoria died in January 1901, India was ruled by Britain, and Calcutta, as Kolkata was then called, was the capital. The viceroy, Lord Curzon, wanted a grand monument for her. He imagined something to match the [[@taj-mahal|Taj Mahal]].

The money came from donations: Indian princes, British officials and members of the public gave about 1 crore and 5 lakh rupees, a vast sum then. The Prince of Wales, later King George V, laid the foundation stone on 4 January 1906.

By the time it opened in December 1921, the capital had already moved to [[@delhi|Delhi]], in 1911. India's freedom struggle was growing fast.

On top of the main dome stands a bronze Angel of Victory, almost 5 metres tall, holding a bugle. It was designed by Emerson's assistant, Vincent Esch, and cast in England.

The angel was mounted so that it could swing around with the wind, like the cockerel on a church weather vane. Over the years it has often been stuck, and getting it turning again has needed careful repair work high above the ground. From the lawns below, the figure looks small. Up close it is taller than two grown adults standing on each other's shoulders.

The memorial has 25 galleries. You can see oil paintings of Indian landscapes by the British uncle and nephew Thomas and William Daniell, who toured India in the 1780s and 1790s. There are portraits, rare books and weapons from the battles of the [[@east-india-company|East India Company]].

Later galleries tell the story of Kolkata itself and of the freedom movement, including the [[@revolt-1857|revolt of 1857]] and the leaders who followed. A building made to honour an [[empire|empire]] now also tells how that empire ended.

Most visitors come as much for the grounds as for the galleries. The gardens hold statues and ponds, and old trees, though Cyclone Amphan knocked several of them down in 2020. Cricket matches happen next door on the Maidan, a huge open park. In the early morning, walkers and joggers circle the outer paths. In the evening, snack sellers wait outside the gates for the crowds.

At night the dome is lit up, and on some evenings there's a light-and-sound show about the city. Not far away, the steel arches of [[@howrah-bridge|Howrah Bridge]] span the Hooghly, the other famous shape on Kolkata's skyline.

text: The Hitopadesha is a collection of fables in [[@sanskrit|Sanskrit]], written by a scholar named Narayana several hundred years ago. Its name means "good advice". It is full of animals who talk, scheme, make friends and fall out: crows, deer, jackals, tigers, pigeons, mice and tortoises.

The book has a clear purpose: to teach wisdom, good sense and the art of ruling. Each story is packed with short verses giving practical advice about friendship, trust, war and peace. For centuries, Indian children learned their first Sanskrit from it. It is still one of the most loved story collections in India.

st.prompt: In a famous Hitopadesha story, a flock of pigeons gets trapped in a hunter's net. How do they escape?

options.t: They all fly up together, carrying the net, to a friend who chews it open
They play dead until the hunter leaves
They peck the net one by one until it breaks

st.reveal: The pigeon king tells his flock to flap at the same moment. Together they lift the whole net into the sky and fly to a mouse friend, who gnaws through the threads. The lesson is that teamwork and true friends can get you out of almost anything.

n.certNote: The Hitopadesha's date is uncertain. It was written by a scholar named Narayana, probably in Bengal, and the oldest dated manuscript was copied in Nepal in 1373. Scholars have suggested dates for the original anywhere from the 9th to the 14th century.

myth: The Hitopadesha is just another name for the Panchatantra.

The two are related, and many Hitopadesha stories come from the Panchatantra. But Narayana arranged them differently, added new tales and many verses of his own, and wrote a separate book with its own character.
facts: good advice, from hita (good) and upadesha (advice)

sec.t:
The book opens with a king named Sudarshana, who ruled at Pataliputra, near today's Patna. He is upset because his sons are lazy and ignorant. A wise teacher called Vishnusharma promises to make them wise within six months.

Instead of boring lessons, he tells them stories. Each story contains other stories inside it, with animals explaining their choices by telling tales of their own. This nested style is very old in India. The [[@panchatantra-tales|Panchatantra]], which uses the same teacher, works the same way, and so do the [[@vikram-betal|Vikram and Betal]] stories.

One famous story begins with a flock of pigeons spotting rice scattered on the ground. The young pigeons rush down to eat, and are caught in a hunter's net. As the hunter approaches, the pigeon king calls out a plan. If they all flap at once, they can lift the net together.

They rise into the sky, net and all, and fly to the king's old friend, a mouse named Hiranyaka. The mouse chews through the threads and sets them free, starting with his friend's subjects before the king himself. A watching [[@crow-smart|crow]] is so impressed that he asks to become the mouse's friend too, and the next story begins.

What makes the Hitopadesha special is its verses. Between the stories, characters quote neat little sayings, often two lines long, much like [[@aesop|Aesop's]] morals but sharper. They warn against trusting flatterers, praise learning above wealth, and point out that a true friend shows up in hard times.

Some sayings are gentle and some are crafty. The book was meant for future rulers, so it teaches how to spot a trick as well as how to be kind. Readers today sometimes find its advice surprisingly modern, especially about choosing [[@friendship|friends]] carefully.

In 1787, Charles Wilkins, an English scholar working in Bengal, published an English [[@translation|translation]] of the Hitopadesha. It was one of the first Sanskrit books translated directly into English. Many more versions followed, in English, German, French and other languages.

For a long time, Sanskrit students in India and abroad began with this book, because its language is fairly simple and its stories are fun. Today, picture books, cartoons and school readers retell its tales in Hindi, Bengali, Tamil and many other languages. Many children who know the pigeons and the net have never heard the book's name.

The Hitopadesha shows how much old Indian storytellers valued cleverness and good company. Its animals are not heroes or villains in a simple way. They make mistakes, trust the wrong people and sometimes learn too late. That mix of humour and honesty is why its stories still get told around Indian dinner tables, centuries after Narayana first wrote them down.

text: Almost every festival in the world has foods that belong to it. Diwali comes with boxes of sweets. Eid comes with bowls of sweet vermicelli. Thanksgiving in the USA means roast turkey, and Lunar New Year in China means dumplings.

These foods usually have a reason behind them. Many follow the seasons, because festivals often mark a harvest or a change in weather. Some carry a meaning, such as sweetness for a happy year or a dish that recalls an old story. Others simply became traditions because families made them year after year. Sharing them with neighbours and friends is often as important as eating them.

st.prompt: In Maharashtra, people hand out sesame and jaggery sweets at Makar Sankranti and say "til-gul ghya, god god bola". What does it mean?

Eat quickly before the sun goes down
Share with your neighbour and get two back

st.reveal: The saying asks people to forget old quarrels and speak kindly in the year ahead. Sesame and jaggery are also warming foods, which suit the middle of winter, when the festival falls.

sec.t:
Many Indian festivals celebrate the harvest, so the food uses fresh crops. In Tamil Nadu, the harvest festival of [[@onam-pongal|Pongal]] shares its name with its main dish. New rice is cooked with milk and [[@jaggery|jaggery]] in a clay or brass pot until it bubbles over the rim. The overflow is a sign of plenty, and people shout "Pongalo Pongal".

In Kerala, the Onam feast called *sadya* is served on a banana leaf, often with more than 20 dishes. There is rice, sambar, avial, thoran, pickles and crispy banana chips, with *payasam*, a sweet pudding, at the end. Each dish has its own place on the leaf. Guests eat with their right hand, and the order in which dishes are served is part of the tradition.

Some festivals involve fasting before the feast. During the holy month of Ramadan, many Muslims eat nothing from dawn to sunset. They often break each day's fast with a date and water, following a practice linked to the Prophet Muhammad, before a bigger evening meal called *iftar*.

When the month ends with [[@eid|Eid]] al-Fitr, many families in South Asia make *sheer khurma* or *seviyan*, vermicelli cooked in sweet milk with nuts and dates. During Navratri, Hindus who fast often skip grains and eat sabudana khichdi or rotis made from buckwheat flour instead.

At Passover, Jewish families eat matzo, a flat bread made without [[yeast|yeast]]. It recalls the story of the Israelites leaving Egypt in such a hurry that their bread had no time to rise. Each food on the special Passover plate stands for a part of that story.

In China and among Chinese families everywhere, Lunar New Year brings dumplings, often shaped like old silver money for good fortune, and long noodles for a long life. [[@thanksgiving|Thanksgiving]] in the USA, held on the fourth Thursday of November, centres on turkey, cranberry sauce and pumpkin pie, foods linked to the American autumn harvest.

Festival foods keep changing. In India, plum cake has become part of [[@christmas|Christmas]], and bakeries in Kerala, Goa and Kolkata are busiest in December. In Japan, where few people are Christian, an advertising campaign in 1974 suggested fried chicken for Christmas. Today, many Japanese families order buckets of it weeks in advance.

Families also bring traditions with them when they move. An Indian family in New Jersey might serve gujiya at Holi and turkey at Thanksgiving. A dish only becomes a festival food when people keep making it, year after year, and teaching it to the next cook in the family.
